documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to draft, summarize, classify, forecast, and communicate information in educational and organizational settings. The resulting governance problem is not limited to model error: AI-generated output becomes consequential when a human accepts, reuses, transmits, or acts on it without review proportionate to the context. This conceptual framework article defines operational AI reliance as the workflow-level process by which a person or institution decides whether and how to use AI-generated output as a basis for action. It develops the SAFER AI™ Protocol as a bounded human-reliance governance framework comprising Scope, Authority, Failure Awareness, Evidence, and Record. The framework does not replace technical assurance, legal compliance, model evaluation, privacy or security controls, or system-level accountability. Its contribution is a user-facing decision routine that connects those controls to the post-generation, pre-action point at which output is evaluated. The article reports an interdisciplinary narrative synthesis of Responsible AI governance, human-centered AI, automation bias, trust calibration, AI literacy, socio-technical governance, and organizational accountability. It then operationalizes the framework through defined terms, a traceability model, a contextual risk classification rubric, an evidence depth scale, and a complete decision flow. The paper concludes with bounded applications in higher education and enterprise work, the framework’s failure mechanisms, and an empirical research agenda that distinguishes verification benefits from implementation burdens. The proposed framework remains conceptual and requires independent empirical evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly incorporated in the life sciences. Until recently, the need for data governance was masked by the limits of our human ability to aggregate, synthesise, and draw inferences from data. AI enhances not only speed of research and data processing, but also dual-use risks from training AI models with open access data. Concerns about AI-enabled chemical and biological weapons development become louder while governments, institutions and model developers scramble to mitigate and contain those risks. Data remains a crucial ingredient for AI model advancement, consequentially the lack of data governance of AI in life sciences leaves us collectively and personally vulnerable. Traditional data governance controls storage, transfer and access to datasets, but AI-enabled life science research raises a different issue: which novel capabilities emerge when models aggregate and orchestrate openly available data and tools, arising from individually benign contributions and not covered by current governance. Thus, we highlight questions and ethical considerations on which precautions are required when risks arise through data aggregation and re-use, how responsibility can be distributed, whether governance should focus on data or novel capabilities and if openness should cease to be default. Data governance works upstream, before data is introduced to an AI model. It follows that more life science dual-use data of concern should be held in Trusted Research Environments rather than released openly, and that dual-use data assessments become routine, implemented through research funders as chokepoints, to bridge the legislative gap until international dual-use standards are established.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

The growing interest in eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has stimulated research on models with built-in interpretability, among which part-prototype models are particularly prominent. Part-Prototype Models (PPMs) classify inputs by comparing them to learned prototypes and provide human-understandable explanations of the form “this looks like that.” Despite this intrinsic interpretability, PPMs have not yet emerged as a competitive alternative to post-hoc explanation methods. This survey reviews work published between 2019 and 2025 and derives a taxonomy of the challenges faced by current PPMs. The analysis reveals a diverse set of open problems. The main issue concerns the quality and number of learned prototypes. Further challenges include limited generalization across tasks and contexts, as well as methodological shortcomings such as non-standardized evaluation. Five broad research directions are identified: improving predictive performance, developing theoretically grounded architectures, establishing frameworks for human-AI collaboration, aligning models with human concepts, and defining robust metrics and benchmarks for evaluation. The survey aims to stimulate further research and promote intrinsically interpretable models for practical applications. A curated list of the surveyed papers is available at https://github.com/aix-group/ppm-survey .

Historically, engineers have been able to certify, explain, and justify the tools they design because they had direct insight into how these tools work. However, the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly those based on neural networks and other models that are not easily explainable, presents a significant ethical challenge: who takes responsibility when neither engineers can explain the tools’ outcome, nor end users can interpret decisions to make informed actions? This “responsibility gap,” caused by the lack of explainability in AI within the context of its increasingly widespread use, demands urgent strategies to mitigate the negative effects of its potential unethical implementations. This article presents a three-tiered approach to reduce the impact of algorithmic opacity: (1) raising social awareness and providing education on the limitations of unexplainable AI systems, (2) creating sector-specific ethical frameworks to guide when (if ever) it is appropriate to use these tools, and (3) establishing a standardized labeling system to indicate the potential limitations and biases of these technologies. Each proposal is evaluated using the AREA framework from Responsible Research & Innovation (Anticipate, Reflect, Engage, Act), allowing us to assess its ethical robustness, societal relevance, and implementation feasibility. The result is a set of conceptual tools designed not to eliminate opacity, but to make it visible, interpretable, and ethically manageable across diverse domains of use.

documents.abstract: This project is a systematic literature review that investigates how conversational agents (CAs; e.g., chatbots and virtual assistants) enact leadership-equivalent behaviors in psychosocial interventions, including therapy, counseling, and coaching. Advances in artificial intelligence have enabled these systems to move beyond process automation and engage in adaptive, relational, and motivational dialogue with users. As such, they increasingly perform functions that parallel those of human leaders, raising important theoretical and practical questions about the nature of leadership when enacted by nonhuman agents. The review has three main purposes. First, it examines which leadership behaviors are effectively exhibited by conversational agents, using Yukl et al.’s (2012) taxonomy of task-, relationship-, change-, and externally-oriented behaviors as an organizing framework. Second, it investigates the mechanisms through which these behaviors exert influence on users in psychosocial contexts, and identifies points of divergence from human-enacted leadership theory. Third, it distills methodological lessons from the existing evidence base, particularly regarding causal trustworthiness, intervention transparency, and replicability, to inform the design of future AI leadership research. The evidence base for this review draws primarily from rigorous experimental and longitudinal studies in medical and behavioral sciences, which provide a strong foundation for assessing agent-enacted influence. Synthesizing this literature, we aim to deliver: - An integrative behavioral framework that maps agent behaviors to leadership theory. - A research agenda outlining methodological standards and open questions for studying AI leadership. - Theoretical refinements that extend leadership theory to account for influence processes enacted by artificial agents. The expected outcome is a comprehensive and causally trustworthy assessment of how conversational agents perform leadership functions in psychosocial interventions, contributing both to leadership theory and to the responsible design of AI systems that increasingly shape workplace interactions.

Measurement–reporting–verification (MRV) is load-bearing wherever claimed contribution must be checked against real contribution — in carbon markets, in the verified-contribution accounting proposed for life-capacity economies, and in audits that classify what objective an AI system appears to pursue. Yet every MRV pipeline rests on a measurer, and a measurer is a trust dependency. The physical world solved a structurally identical problem decades ago: no single satellite, sensor tower, or field plot is trusted to estimate carbon stock; heterogeneous modalities with different bias profiles are triangulated, and disagreement between them is information, not noise. We instantiate the same pattern for AI normative audits. Our pipeline combines three measurement modalities — LLM judge families (remote, scalable, biased), a human gold set (local, expensive, ground-truth), and revealed-preference behavioral tasks — behind preregistered gates that can fail and be reported, a scorer-of-record selected by coded-seed agreement, and a published rejected-instrument exhibit. Applied to a 4,164-record audit of open-weight model objectives, the system localizes exactly which judgment is contested: judge–human agreement is Cohen's κ=0.22 overall, but failure concentrates on the boundary question ("does this text presume an objective at all," κ≈0.19) while direction survives (φ-share 29.8% human vs 25.5% judge on the jointly objective-bearing subset). We therefore report magnitudes as judge-family quantities and direction as a cross-modal finding — decomposition reporting that binds each claim to the level its weakest instrument supports. Part of the LESS–IS–MORE program.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Trust remains insufficiently understood in construction AI, particularly where AI outputs inform safety-critical or contractual decisions with professional and legal consequences. This study investigates how construction professionals evaluate and justify trust under technical uncertainty, site variability and professional accountability. A cross-national mixed-methods design was used to analyse 1,233 valid survey responses from professionals in managerial, technical, design and site-based roles across Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The study distinguishes trust calibration, defined as aligning trust with an AI system’s capabilities and limitations, from calibrated professional reliance, whereby AI outputs are relied upon only when they are technically reliable, contextually appropriate and professionally defensible. Across the three countries, accuracy, reliability and contextual alignment formed the basis for reliance, while governance, explainability, transparency and accountability supported reliance under safety, contractual and regulatory scrutiny. The main risks concerned unreliable predictions and data privacy and security, while the main benefits were efficiency, planning accuracy and decision support. The study advances trust-in-AI research by conceptualizing calibrated professional reliance as a construction-specific judgement shaped by technical performance, contextual fit and professional accountability. These findings explain how construction professionals decide whether to accept, verify, modify, override or reject AI outputs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital impersonation exploits trust, verification behavior, and decision-making under uncertainty. This structured narrative review synthesizes selected literature on cybersecurity, social engineering, trust in automation, AI-mediated communication, and synthetic media. Four themes organize the analysis: trust calibration, cognitive biases and social influence, verification failure, and human-centered defenses. The literature suggests that susceptibility reflects interactions among credibility cues, authority pressure, urgency, cognitive demands, and organizational practices. Generative AI can reproduce familiar communication cues, challenging verification based on appearance, fluency, or sensory familiarity. However, evidence from conventional phishing and automation research does not establish the magnitude of these effects in every AI-enabled setting. The review proposes research priorities addressing trust measurement, verification fatigue, organizational culture, and interactive deception. Its central implication is that effective defense requires usable verification procedures and organizational support alongside technical detection and training.

This study examines the factors associated with university students’ decisions to use artificial intelligence (AI) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, drawing on an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Data were collected from 369 students across 40 universities, including 53 international students (14.36%), and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings support all seven hypothesized direct relationships. Facilitating conditions are positively associated with perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while perceived ease of use is positively related to perceived usefulness and intention to use. Perceived usefulness shows the strongest direct association with behavioral intention (β = 0.534), whereas intention to use is the strongest direct predictor of self-reported AI usage decisions (β = 0.480). Significant indirect effects further highlight the interconnected roles of technological perceptions and behavioral intention. The study contributes to technology acceptance research by examining reported AI usage decisions alongside behavioral intention within a higher education setting involving students from different national backgrounds. The findings suggest that universities, instructors, and student support services should strengthen access to AI tools, provide responsible-use guidance, and consider multilingual academic support. Because the analysis uses pooled, cross-sectional data, the findings do not establish causal relationships or international student-specific effects.

Family-centered care coordination (FC-CC) in pediatric rehabilitation benefits from tools that support caregivers in contributing to personalized service planning for their children. Participation and Environment Measure (PEM) is a digital application that is being further developed to support FC-CC in early intervention (EI). PEM is being further developed to include the Young Children’s Participation and Environment Measure (YC-PEM) electronic patient-reported outcome and a companion PEM-Plus (PEM+) goal setting intervention. This study examined usability of the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled PEM prototype. Caregivers from an urban EI program met these eligibility criteria: (1) were at least 18 years old; (2) identified as the parent or legal guardian of a child enrolled in EI services; (3) read, wrote, and spoke English; (4) had internet and telephone access; and (5) had a child 0–3 years old who received EI services for 3 or more months. Participants completed the AI-enabled PEM application with access to a debiased prototypic conversational agent. PEM usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS), and chatbot usability was assessed along four BOT Usability Scale (BUS-11) domains: 1) accessibility of chatbot functions; 2) functional interactive conversation; 3) privacy and security; and 4) timely response. Univariate logistic regression models were used to examine associations between each of the four BUS-11 domains and PEM+ engagement. Eleven female caregivers of children (mean age: 24.5 months) enrolled, 66.7% of whom interacted with the prototypic chatbot during one or more iterations of the PEM+ intervention. Overall PEM usability remained acceptable. While overall chatbot usability was very poor (Mdn = 53.4%, IQR = 50.0, 55.4), caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability were average for accessibility of chatbot functions (Mdn = 3.8, IQR = 3.0, 4.0) and good for privacy and security ( M = 3.1, Range = 2.0–5.0). Higher caregiver perceptions of chatbot usability did not significantly increase odds of PEM+ intervention use. Findings indicate that an AI-enabled PEM retains adequate usability. A chatbot integrated within the PEM+ intervention is accessible and secure, though its functional interactive conversation and timely responses could benefit from further development to increase odds of its use in an EI service context. documents.abstract: This study analyzed Production Engineering students’ use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) at FT/UFAM, Brazil, in the first semester of 2026 to support pedagogical decisions. This exploratory, descriptive, and quantitative study surveyed 106 of the 263 enrolled students through non-probability convenience sampling. Course- level responses were screened with consistency rules based on institutional documents and analyzed using descriptive statistics, a chi-square test, and generalized estimating equations. In all, 87.7% of respondents use GenAI, mainly ChatGPT and Gemini, to improve their writing and solve problems. Differences between semester blocks varied across data-screening scenarios, which precludes conclusions about a pattern of use throughout the program. Among users, 63% learned to use these tools on their own and only 16% from university instructors; 68% reported difficulties with GenAI literacy and 61% a lack of clear guidelines. Among respondents, widespread GenAI adoption contrasts with the limited role of instructors as a reported source of learning and with the absence of program- specific guidelines: the central challenge is not to introduce GenAI but to provide pedagogical guidance for a practice that is already widespread. We recommend combining AI literacy, explicit rules in course syllabi, and assessments that value the learning process and transparency of use.

As large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape children’s learning, fostering informed and critical engagement has become an urgent educational task. This study examines children’s AI literacy and trust in LLMs during a learning interaction. Thirty children aged 8-10 years participated in semi-structured interviews combined with an interaction task using a customized LLM. Children used the system competently, yet their conceptual understanding remained fragmented. At the same time, children placed high trust in the LLM’s ability and benevolence, while perceptions of integrity, particularly regarding data privacy, were more cautious. Their reasoning was frequently anthropomorphic, reinforced by social cues such as natural language use and emojis. The human analogy, however, was applied selectively. Children explained the system’s errors through human fallibility, but most considered algorithmic bias impossible, treating prejudice as a uniquely human trait. These findings suggest that AI literacy education should begin in elementary school and explicitly address questions of fairness, building on children’s intuition that AI learns from humans.

documents.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnel across a broad range of fields and populations who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.

This practice-based and philosophical paper reflects on human collaboration with AI agents, especially for learning expert-level skills in higher education. Using the development of the AI-supported multi-agent system LASSI as an example, it narrates a learning journey in three phases: productive amazement, a shift in authorship, and finally taking responsibility. Perspectives of a developer, a professor, and students show how human-agent systems change through collaboration. Three philosophical dimensions – embodied knowledge, enhanced technologies, and embedded ethics – are used to assess potentials and risks: what happens when intelligence is disembodied, human capabilities are outsourced to technology, and values are encoded? The paper argues that agents should not be treated as neutral tools but as co-shapers within the sociotechnical system of education. It concludes by portraying universities as thinking workshops that must redefine their role with AI: away from exam-driven routines toward cultivating judgment and self-reflection.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

The spread of generative AI has made "brain outsourcing"—delegating cognitive tasks to AI—a common phenomenon in higher education, especially in low-tier private undergraduate colleges. Existing studies explain it mainly at the individual level, neglecting the institutional consequences of the technologies used to govern it. Drawing on design-based research principles, this study conducted a three-group quasi-experiment in a Data Structures course at such a college: an adversarial workflow (Group A, n = 36), a negotiative workflow (Group B, n = 40), and a traditional control group (n = 44), triangulated across five chains of evidence. Results show that Group A's direct-dumping rate fell to 11.1% (vs. 57.5% and 75.0%), yet concealed forms—cosmetic modification and division-of-labor outsourcing—rose compensatorily, leaving the composite outsourcing index unchanged across groups (p = 0.864). Process engagement rose sharply while output authenticity stayed low (comment–code matching 3.62/5; only 27.8% of difficulty tags authentic), indicating "performative engagement". Only 1 of 120 students adopted a self-regulated strategy. In Group A, perceived control rose (+2.17) and negotiation space fell (−0.91) without meaningful growth in autonomy; the 18.3-point advantage over the control group in comprehension depth shrank to 6.8 points in transfer application. The "non-outsourceable" workflow thus changed outsourcing's form, not its deep structure, alienating learning into an adversarial game of evading detection—a new hidden curriculum. Agent design should shift from adversarial surveillance to dialogic support.

Problematic social media use (PSMU) among adolescents has raised significant concerns due to its widespread prevalence and close association with broad maladjustment. The existing literature suggests that bullying victimization could be an important risk factor driving PSMU, with well-being indicators (e.g., life satisfaction) as a typical mediation pathway. However, how individual psychological assets (e.g., interpersonal strengths) may modify the link between bullying victimization, life satisfaction, and PSMU is less clear. This study investigated a two-stage moderated mediation model linking bullying victimization to PSMU, with life satisfaction serving as the mediator and interpersonal strengths as the moderator. Based on data collected from 2,400 Chinese adolescents, the results showed that (a) bullying victimization was positively associated with PSMU, (b) bullying victimization was negatively related to life satisfaction, which in turn was negatively associated with PSMU, and (c) interpersonal strengths amplified the link between bullying victimization and life satisfaction and that between life satisfaction and PSMU; consequently, interpersonal strengths enhanced the mediating role of life satisfaction and the total effect of bullying victimization on PSMU. Our findings advance our understanding of the moderated mediation mechanism that links bullying victimization to adolescents’ PSMU. In particular, this study highlights the context-dependent nature of interpersonal strengths as a promotive factor in general but exerting a reverse risk-buffering (exacerbating) effect in the context of bullying victimization and PSMU.

Abstract Studies have examined the impact of Generative AI (GenAI) on students’ learning outcomes, revealing a wide range of effects on performance, cognitive load, and learning processes. However, little is known about whether these effects change with learner expertise and the conditions under which GenAI support is provided. This study examined expertise reversal in GenAI-supported programming education across four eight-week experiments involving Year 3 computer science students from research universities in Saudi Arabia. Drawing on cognitive load theory, the experiments investigated GenAI support, guidance level, task complexity, and access condition in relation to intrinsic cognitive load, extraneous cognitive load, mental effort, and independent programming performance. The findings showed that GenAI support produced greater reductions in extraneous load and stronger independent performance among lower-expertise learners, while higher-expertise learners retained smaller benefits. Detailed guidance produced a crossover expertise reversal, benefiting lower-expertise learners while increasing extraneous load and weakening performance among higher-expertise learners. Higher task complexity increased cognitive demands and reduced performance across expertise levels, with greater effects among lower-expertise learners. Personalised access also benefited lower-expertise learners more strongly without disadvantaging higher-expertise learners. Overall, the findings distinguish a crossover expertise reversal under detailed GenAI guidance from diminishing benefits as learner expertise increases under other support and access conditions. The effects of task complexity further demonstrate that expertise-dependent differences do not necessarily constitute a reversal in instructional effectiveness. We recommend that effective GenAI support requires careful calibration to learners’ existing knowledge and the cognitive demands of learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Mindsponge theory (MT) holds that the mind evaluates incoming information most thoroughly when it neither trusts nor distrusts the source, and least at either extreme. Its testing program states this as prediction P2: the weight that content carries in acceptance follows an inverted U across trust. Rival accounts expect the weight to stay constant (Bayesian combination) or to rise with trust (monotone moderation). We report the first admitted test of P2, on the open Human-AI Interactions dataset of Vodrahalli et al. (2022). In that study, 207 US adults judged the art period of 32 paintings, received advice described as 65% or 95% accurate (identical advice in both groups), and gave a final answer. Because participants were about 66 to 70% accurate on their own, the 65% source sits near indifference and the 95% source is highly trusted, so the design covers the trusted half of the curve, where MT predicts that content weight falls. The rule, fixed and fingerprinted before any final answer was read, measured how strongly a participant’s own first judgment of the advised label governed whether the final answer sided with the advice. The weight was 4.42 logits at 65% and 3.43 at 95%; the difference was 0.99 (SE 0.34, z = 2.94, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.65), and the verdict is supported. Adding a 65/80/95 comparison gives 4.43, 3.68 and 3.45. The result survives two-way clustering and alternative codings. A post-verdict decomposition shows that trust mattered only when people’s own judgment opposed the advice; within those trials the drop in weight is clearer on a continuous measure (z = 2.17) than on the pre-specified binary one (z = 0.64). Because trials in which participants already agreed with the advice cannot show acceptance, these disagreement trials are the cleaner test of P2. The result clearly disfavors monotone moderation, disfavors constant Bayesian weighting with moderate rather than strong evidence, and does not separate MT from simple opinion averaging. It supports the trusted half of P2, not the full inverted U.

Generative AI systems are increasingly used to retrieve, synthesize, evaluate, and communicate information in knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet observed epistemic performance is often attributed either to the human user or to the AI model, even when it depends on a wider configuration of models, retrieval mechanisms, external sources, tools, interfaces, permissions, and human oversight. This paper asks under what conditions epistemic capacity should be attributed to a configured system rather than to either the human or the model alone, and what follows from locating that capacity. Drawing on distributed cognition, extended and social epistemology, and work on epistemic technologies, the paper develops a task-relative attribution framework grounded in functional externalization. For a specified task class, operating conditions, and acceptable performance criterion, it identifies a minimal adequate capacity-bearing configuration as an organized set of functionally integrated components sufficient to realize the relevant capacity, such that no proper subconfiguration remains sufficient under the same specification. Minimality does not imply uniqueness: different configurations may be equally minimal and adequate. Through comparative functional reconstruction of context-bounded synthesis, retrieval-augmented generation, and tool-augmented systems, the paper distinguishes operational components from epistemic resources and background conditions and shows why individual component necessity is not required when redundant routes realize the same functional role. The paper advances two claims. First, epistemic capacity should be attributed at the minimal organized level required to explain its realization across the relevant class of tasks, rather than inferred from the most visible component. Second, locating that capacity does not determine the loci of understanding, epistemic authority, purpose, control, authorship, or responsibility. These properties may coincide with, overlap, or diverge from the capacity-bearing configuration, but only for independent reasons. The contribution is therefore not to rediscover distributed cognition or sociotechnical epistemic practice, but to provide a deliberately minimal framework for disciplined attribution without presupposing a theory of extended mind, artificial understanding, or epistemic subjecthood.

Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI is being used extensively by destination marketing organisations (DMOs) to create promotional imagery, and new regulation requires disclosure of some synthetic content. Previous research indicates that revealing an AI source can reduce perceived authenticity but treats disclosure as a single cue. This study investigated whether travellers react differently when the AI label is presented as the DMO's own decision or as a legally mandated requirement. A simulated single factor, three condition (no label, voluntary label, mandated label) between-subjects online experiment with N = 387 adult participants. The analysis was based on the Persuasion Knowledge Model and attribution theory, using ANCOVA, bootstrapped parallel mediation analyses (multicategorical predictor), moderation by attitudes towards AI and robustness checks. Both labels reduced perceived authenticity compared to no label (voluntary: d = −0.59; mandated: d = −0.74). The voluntary label raised perceived DMO integrity (d = 0.38), producing a positive indirect effect on visit intention. The mandated label earned no integrity credit, and its negative indirect effect through authenticity was not compensated. These effects were not significantly moderated by general attitudes toward AI. The study distinguishes between what the AI label says and who is seen to have chosen it, thereby furthering the research on persuasion-knowledge in tourism and providing a model that DMOs can test for disclosure in the regulatory era.

documents.abstract: "AI safety" has grown from a niche contingent of actors into the dominant framing for artificial intelligence (AI) assessment and evaluation, overshadowing AI ethics. Through political and monetary influence, AI safety has shifted political focus within the US and abroad. The focus has shifted away from harms that currently affect the public toward threats framed as "existential risks". We argue that safety cannot be achieved while anti-Blackness is left unaddressed. We ground this argument in Sylvia Wynter's critique of the "overrepresentation" of Man: the modern, Western conception of the Human that is predicated on the subjugation and othering of Blackness. To analyze the state of addressing anti-Blackness in the age of AI safety, we conduct a two-stage, language model-assisted content analysis of 69,290 accepted main-track papers from ten leading machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), and AI ethics conferences (2020--2025). Safety research grew from 0.5% of accepted papers in 2020 to 6.4% in 2025, overtaking ethics. Yet 94% of safety papers rely on automated metrics, and only 11% of safety papers mention harms that affect society directly, compared with 78% of ethics papers. Of the 2,182 safety papers, 8 mention race; none make it central, and none name Black or African-diaspora communities. Across all 254 identified as race-focused papers, only 3 describe racial harm in safety terms, and 55% appear at three ethics venues that publish 2.5% of the corpus. We offer this interdisciplinary examination of AI safety to argue that a just technological future depends on confronting anti-Blackness directly.

documents.abstract: Abstract Organizations continue investing trillions of dollars in artificial intelligence (AI), yet many fail to realize meaningful business value. This article argues that the primary barrier to successful AI transformation is not the technology itself, but a widespread leadership misconception …

Artificial intelligence is forcing education to confront a question that long predates AI: What is education ultimately for? Modern educational systems have become highly effective at transmitting knowledge, developing analytical capacity, and preparing young people for further education and employment. These are important achievements. Yet they represent only part of what education can do for a human being. When education is organized primarily around knowledge acquisition, competition, assessment, and selection, the development of the person as a whole can become secondary. The emergence of artificial intelligence makes this limitation increasingly visible. Machines can already store, retrieve, synthesize, and process information at a scale no human being can or should attempt to match. If education continues to define human development primarily in terms of information processing and analytical performance, it risks preparing young people to compete with machines in domains in which machines will increasingly excel. I propose a different direction: Wisdom-Based Education. Wisdom-Based Education places the cultivation of the whole human being alongside intellectual development as a fundamental purpose of education. Drawing upon Ren Xue, a contemporary system of human development rooted in Chinese wisdom traditions, it views the human being as an integrated totality of Body, Qi, and Jingshen (composite of consciousness, heart and True Self) and proposes that education should deliberately cultivate self-awareness, inner stability, health, ethical discernment, compassion, creativity, wisdom, and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to others. Its central hypothesis is that wisdom is not merely the accidental product of age or experience. Capacities associated with wisdom can be intentionally cultivated. This proposition changes what we teach, how we teach, how teachers understand their role, how parents participate in education, how children learn from relationships, and how we define educational success. Academic learning remains essential, but it becomes part of a larger developmental process directed toward five broad outcomes: health, happiness, wellbeing, continuing growth, and meaningful contribution. This paper presents the philosophical foundations of Wisdom-Based Education, its model of human development, its implications for educational practice, and a pathway through which its propositions can be translated into curricula, pilot programs, teacher and parent preparation, and systematic research. Its fundamental claim is simple: the next transformation of education must be concerned not merely with what human beings know, but with what human beings can become.

Introduction: Workplace flexibility has emerged as a critical concern for contemporary organizations, particularly as they seek to attract and retain Generation Z employees, who enter the labor market with distinct expectations regarding autonomy and wellbeing. Although research suggests that workplace flexibility fosters positive employee outcomes and helps address the growing challenge of quiet quitting, critical questions remain about the mechanisms through which these practices operate. Specifically, it remains unclear whether the different dimensions of workplace flexibility (temporal, operational, functional, and workspace) influence quiet quitting solely through an indirect pathway, by strengthening work engagement, or also through direct effects, and whether these mechanisms operate similarly across all four dimensions. Methods A quantitative research strategy was used to collect data from 401 Generation Z employees working in Lithuania during 2026. The questionnaire was distributed through an online, self-administered survey. The data was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and mediation analysis with Hayes' PROCESS Model 4. Results Hypothesis testing revealed that temporal flexibility showed the largest standardized coefficients in absolute terms for both work engagement and quiet quitting, followed by operational flexibility; functional flexibility significantly predicted quiet quitting but not work engagement, while workspace flexibility showed a small significant association with work engagement but no significant unique association with quiet quitting. Work engagement significantly and negatively related to quiet quitting (β = −0.515, p < 0.001). The indirect effects of temporal and operational flexibility through work engagement were statistically significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations, whereas no significant mediation was found for functional or workspace flexibility. Discussion These findings contribute to theoretical understanding by demonstrating that different flexibility dimensions exhibit distinct direct and indirect statistical associations with quiet quitting, with significant indirect associations through work engagement for temporal and operational flexibility. This pattern aligns with the Job Demands-Resources model, revealing that not all flexibility dimensions operate through the same mechanism. Practically, results indicate that organizations seeking to reduce quiet quitting among Generation Z employees should prioritize temporal and operational flexibility as strategic investments with direct impact on both work engagement and quiet quitting.

Although robots are increasingly reshaping organizational workflows, how the robot proportion in human-robot teams affects employees’ turnover intention remains underexplored. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we examine whether, why, and when robot proportion exerts divergent effects on turnover intention through two pathways: resource gain and resource loss. Evidence from a scenario-based experiment (Study 1, N = 290) and a three-wave field study (Study 2, N = 306) reveals that these two pathways operate in opposing directions. Specifically, work goal progress and work loneliness mediate the relationship between robot proportion in human-robot teams and turnover intention. Robot anthropomorphism further moderates these pathways: higher anthropomorphism strengthens the beneficial effect on work goal progress, whereas lower anthropomorphism amplifies the detrimental effect on work loneliness. This study offers initial evidence on how the structural composition of human-robot teams shapes employees’ turnover intention, and it provides practical implications for organizations deploying robotic coworkers.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in academic and professional work, yet ethical debate has focused on whether specific uses are acceptable rather than whether people judge those uses consistently. This paper introduces AI Moral Exceptionalism (AIME), the tendency of individuals or institutions to view their own AI use as ethically legitimate while applying stricter standards to substantively equivalent uses by others, a form of self–other double standard. Drawing on research on self-serving bias, moral hypocrisy, motivated reasoning, and moral licensing, the paper defines AIME, distinguishes it from hypocrisy and legitimate ethical differentiation, and identifies four forms: competence, intentional, contribution, and institutional exceptionalism. It proposes four conceptual pathways through which these judgments may arise: asymmetric contextual knowledge, framing AI as assistance for oneself but as substitution for others, perceived competence, and reputational norms. To distinguish justified differences in judgment from preferential ones, it introduces the AI Moral Exceptionalism Diagnostic (AIMED), which examines behavioural equivalence, normative equivalence, evaluative consistency, and justificatory adequacy. The analysis concludes that responsible AI governance requires actor-neutral standards, context-sensitive assessment, and symmetrical accountability, ensuring that those who set and enforce AI-use rules are held to the standards they apply to others. The paper is conceptual; it identifies implications for academic integrity, AI-use disclosure, and workplace practice, and sets out directions for empirical testing.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study explores how employees in Saudi Arabian organisations perceive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven human resource management (HRM) and how their interpretations of the technology shape trust in HR systems and employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach: This qualitative study draws on 35 semi-structured interviews analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings: Employees’ perceptions of AI-driven HRM were shaped by transparency, human involvement, and contextual sensitivity. Employees expressed conditional trust in AI used for administrative tasks, but were more reluctant to trust it with consequential decisions such as performance appraisals. Concerns about dignity, autonomy, and mental well-being were closely linked to perceptions of AI-driven HRM as context-blind and overly reductive. Originality/value: By placing employee sensemaking at the centre of the analysis, this study clarifies how AI-driven HRM is interpreted in organisational settings and how such interpretations shape trust and well-being. Practical implications: The study highlights the need for a hybrid HRM model that combines technological efficiency with transparency, contextual awareness, and meaningful human oversight.

documents.abstract: The deployment of AI systems in healthcare demands explanations tailored to healthcare professionals’ (HCPs’) decision-making processes and clinical contexts. XAI approaches often fail to influence clinical behavior because they lack audience adaptation and multidisciplinary integration. This paper presents a human-centered explainability (HCXAI) framework that integrates XAI throughout the complete AI system lifecycle rather than as a post-hoc addition. The framework extends existing Human-Centered AI (HCAI) methodologies by adopting a triple diamond approach and explicitly positioning explainability activities across six development phases around three complementary dimensions: human (HCPs, aligned with BLUE XAI), technical (developers and researchers, aligned with RED XAI), and legal (regulatory compliance with EU AI Act). HCP information needs are characterized based on clinical reasoning stages and contextual factors such as activity type, time constraints, error consequences, protocol usage, and user expertise. Each phase produces documentary outputs contributing to EU AI Act Articles 9, 11, 13, and 14 compliance. The framework is illustrated through a retrospective analysis of NaIA-RD, a diabetic retinopathy screening AI system deployed in clinical practice.

documents.abstract: This paper reports ongoing work at La Trobe University to cultivate a shared understanding of effective artificial intelligence (AI) integration through the design of a human-centred framework for embedding AI literacies into teaching and learning. In response to conceptual ambiguity of AI curriculum integration, the Online Education Design team developed an operational definition positioning AI as infrastructure for active learning and the educator as the central decision-maker in the learning design process. This definition was translated into the AI-Informed Learning Design Framework, a four-step process, in which educators define the learning goal, select an AI pedagogical role, apply an AI Assessment Scale boundary check, then design learning activities that develop disciplinary knowledge and AI literacy. Supported by a four-level scaffolding model governing students' growing independence in AI use, the framework was piloted through two rounds, using a design-based research methodology. Feedback from Round one highlighted opportunities to refine the framework whilst also emphasising broader sector-wide tensions surrounding AI integration, including educators’ reluctance to use AI and concerns about the framing of some AI roles in teaching and learning. Early findings from the second round suggest improved educator engagement and a stronger understanding of the framework.

documents.abstract: The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is often framed as though we are adapting from a stable baseline. In reality, teaching and assessment practices were already significantly reshaped by the pandemic, a period that demanded compassion, accessibility, and rapid digital transformation (Hodges et al., 2020; UNESCO, 2020). While these shifts improved equity and inclusion, they also normalised highly prescriptive assessment approaches, limiting space for creativity and learner agency (Armoed, 2021; Sambell & Brown, 2021). As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) now moves from pandemic-driven adaptation toward AI-integrated learning, these inherited practices warrant reconsideration: approaches designed to provide structure and safeguard integrity may inadvertently constrain the agency, experimentation and authentic engagement that emerging technologies make possible. This presentation challenges the idea that AI is the first major disruption in higher education and presents it as a catalyst that exposes long-standing tensions between guidance and autonomy, support and trust, and structure and freedom within TEL contexts (Eaton, 2020; Selwyn, 2023). Drawing on an integrated theoretical foundation of social constructivism, heutagogy, and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework (TPACK), it introduces the need for an innovative mindset shift from a pedagogy of protection toward a pedagogy of trust (Cole et al., 1978; Hase & Kenyon, 2000; Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Applied to assessment design, social constructivism foregrounds dialogue and co-construction, heutagogy supports learner agency and self-determined engagement with AI, and TPACK guides purposeful alignment between emerging technologies, pedagogy and disciplinary knowledge. Aligned with the Human-Centred Learning Design theme, this presentation offers a conceptual lens for rethinking assessment in AI-integrated environments, one that prioritises relationships, learner agency, and co-created integrity. Using strong visual storytelling true to the Pecha Kucha format, the session traces a path from pandemic-era learning and assessment design to the current AI landscape and beyond, highlighting how each moment has reshaped our relationship with knowledge, teaching, and our perceptions of academic integrity. Attendants are invited to reflect on where control-driven practices persist in their own assessment approaches and explore how greater learner choice, transparent AI engagement and co-created expectations for integrity might enable more trust-based, ethically engaged approaches to learning (Bovill, 2020). The challenge is no longer how we protect learning from technology, but how we design for trust, transformation, and future-ready education.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.

Understanding the decision-making process of machine learning models has driven significant advances in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Feature attribution methods play a central role in explaining model behavior, yet selecting an appropriate method remains challenging due to the wide range of available techniques and the lack of standardized evaluation metrics. Without clear selection criteria, practitioners risk choosing suboptimal or misleading explanations. This survey addresses this challenge by providing a structured synthesis of the evaluation landscape. We introduce a multi-layer framework that organizes evaluation metrics into model-centric, explanation-centric, and human-centric layers, providing a systematic perspective for assessing feature attribution methods. We present practical guidelines to support practitioners in selecting appropriate methods based on this framework, while acknowledging the inherent context-dependency of method performance. We also identify open challenges in the field, including metric inconsistencies, trade-offs between explanation properties, and the integration of computational and human-centered evaluations. Our findings underscore the need for more formalized selection strategies and practical deployment frameworks, bridging the gap between theoretical advancements and real-world applications.

Despite a proliferation of research on GenAI for second/foreign language (L2) education since the official launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, current understanding of its role in L2 oral proficiency development remains limited. To address this research gap, this systematic review draws on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine how GenAI may support L2 learners’ three basic psychological needs and how such need satisfaction may be associated with their cognitive, behavioural, and emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking. Adopting the PRISMA Statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses) approach, the review identified 30 empirical studies from ProQuest, Web of Science, and Scopus based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected studies were analysed using a hybrid deductive and inductive coding approach following a coding framework. The analysis suggests that GenAI can enhance L2 learners’ sense of autonomy satisfaction by enabling learner-driven choices and interaction personalisation. It may also support competence satisfaction by affording accessible oral practice, immediate and personalised feedback, and scaffolded speaking development. Regarding relatedness satisfaction, GenAI appears to offer partial support by providing a non-judgemental and emotionally supportive practice environment. Furthermore, the degree of needs satisfaction may be associated with learners’ behavioural, cognitive, and emotional engagement (or disengagement) in GenAI-supported L2 speaking development. Specifically, the findings suggest that emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking appears most evident, followed by cognitive and behavioural engagement. These findings extend the SDT literature in GenAI-assisted language learning and offer practical insights for integrating emerging technologies into language education. For educators, given the review highlights the promising affordances of GenAI to address conventional barriers to L2 oral proficiency development, teachers should integrate GenAI into speaking classes to create an anxiety-free and feedback-rich speaking practice environment, while they need to consider learners’ age and proficiency to provide necessary teacher guidance.

In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

documents.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

documents.abstract: This paper reports preliminary findings from a redesigned capstone assessment in a first-year Management unit at an Australian university involving over 300 students. Rather than treating generative AI as a content-generation tool, the assessment positions it as a simulated interview partner within a three-phase architecture: a pre-interview strategy memo, an AI-conducted adaptive interview, and a post-interview reflective analysis. Grounded in Schön’s reflective practice framework and Biggs and Tang’s constructive alignment, the design surfaces the gap between how students plan to communicate and how they do. Preliminary thematic analysis of 21 student reflective submissions reveals four patterns: (a) the strategy memo functions as a metacognitive anchor, making the gap between intention and execution visible and diagnosable; (b) students consistently demonstrate framework knowledge but revert to habitual communication patterns under adaptive pressure; (c) the structured reflection phase produces sophisticated self-diagnostic reasoning that connects transcript evidence to communication theory; and (d) students who completed multiple simulation attempts used iterative practice as a developmental mechanism rather than a remedial exercise. These findings suggest that AI-simulated interviews, when embedded within a reflective assessment architecture, generate qualitatively richer professional learning than traditional scripted interview preparation.

Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming ubiquitous in consumers' lives and search activities. AI applications that can create content, have conversations, respond to emotions, recognize images and objects, and construct real‐world experiences (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Google Lens, Apple Vision Pro) are transforming consumer search by functioning as psychological surrogates that assume key cognitive, evaluative, perceptual, and relational processes on consumers' behalf. Yet limited research has examined how these technologies transform the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer search. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic narrative review of 75 articles on the psychological foundations of consumer search and introduces the concept of AI psychological surrogacy, which happens when advanced‐AI technologies assume key psychological processes traditionally performed by humans. We develop a conceptual framework that theorizes AI psychological surrogacy across three higher‐order systems (affective‐relational delegation, cognitive‐evaluative substitution, and sensory‐perceptual construction) and six mechanisms: affective transference, relational surrogacy, cognitive delegation, evaluative surrogacy, perceptual offloading, and sensory augmentation. We advance six research propositions and a research agenda for investigating how reliance on AI as a psychological surrogate may alter consumer cognition, evaluation, perception, and relational dynamics.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Responsible human resource management (HRM) relies on human oversight, which works only when people are willing to question problematic algorithmic outputs. Based on social cognitive theory and psychological safety theory, this study investigates whether there is a direct link between AI literacy and the ethical voice in algorithms for hiring, as well as whether there is an indirect link through psychological safety and moral efficacy. Data of the survey in the form of information was collected from 390 employees who were engaged in recruitment and selection process in four multinational companies in Pakistan (purposive sampling; 470 questionnaires were distributed). The regression and bootstrap analyses revealed that the variables of psychological safety (B = 0.31) and moral efficacy (B = 0.37) had a positive relationship with AI literacy, while the direct path from ethical voice to AI literacy showed a stronger effect (total effect B = 0.44, p < .001). Psychological safety and moral efficacy both predicted ethical voice, and there was an indirect relationship between psychological safety and moral efficacy. Indirect effects made up approximately 42% of the overall effect, and there were significant indirect paths via psychological safety, via moral efficacy, and sequentially via both psychological safety and moral efficacy, in addition to a significant direct path (complementary partial mediation). AI-literacy training in combination with a safe reporting climate and high moral efficacy might therefore be most likely to help supervise ethical use. Data are cross-sectional in nature and self-reported, so the results are interpreted in terms of associations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection systems can enhance visual search in safety-critical domains, yet how they present recommendations may determine their effectiveness under display-quality constraints. We compared three cueing methods: an indirect cue signaling only presence (textual alert) and two direct cues marking the target’s location through either signal enhancement (bounding box) or noise reduction (contextual blur), across color and monochrome displays. Participants (N = 122) searched maritime aerial imagery in a fixed-order block structure (unaided, aided, unaided). Direct cues improved detection only under monochrome conditions, whereas the indirect cue lowered joint human–AI accuracy below that of the AI alone. Bounding boxes yielded the highest detection, whereas contextual blur reduced response times and increased compliance. Temporal analyses revealed that aided performance diverged from retained skill, with blur the most durable after withdrawal despite stronger signs of automation dependence. Cueing should be matched to display type and operational context, and judged by the skill that persists after support.

This article explores the innovative potential of generative artificial intelligence in distance education and focuses on its application to enhance teaching practice and student learning. The concept of AI-enabled pedagogy is introduced, where lecturers utilise generative artificial intelligence tools to create personalised, adaptive, and immersive learning experiences. A case study of a distance education module illustrates the effective integration of generative artificial intelligence in teaching practices and highlights its benefits in the automation of repetitive tasks, provision of synchronous feedback, and the facilitation of collaborative learning. The article also examines the challenges and limitations of implementing generative artificial intelligence in distance education which include concerns related to academic integrity, bias, and digital literacy. The findings of this study include perspectives into the potential of generative artificial intelligence to transform teaching and learning in distance education. The article provides implications for lecturers, policymakers, and researchers, and highlights future directions for research on GAI in distance education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and discriminant validity thresholds. Human-AI task complementarity is the strongest proximal predictor of productivity and performance, followed at some distance by trust in AI and by job insecurity, which carries a negative sign. AI governance and reskilling investment have indirect effects, albeit small but reliable, that are passed on through the process of trust. However, job insecurity undermines the complementarity-performance relationship, although the interaction does not contribute much (under one percent) to the explained variance and should be avoided. The two phases imply that investment in artificial intelligence to boost productivity primarily is reshaping jobs and the context in which they exist.
