documents.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.

Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system’s output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

Convincing digital copies of professional selves, avatars that look, sound, and respond like a person, have become easier to produce with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). This paper reports work in progress on a postgraduate business subject at an Australian university, in which students explore professional identity by constructing, testing, and questioning AI representations of themselves. In a curriculum-embedded workshop, students choose between two equivalent activities: building an AI avatar from a self-authored knowledge base or writing a structured professional profile. Both ask students to decide deliberately what to share with, and withhold from, an AI system, then to test their representation against simulated professional scenarios before reflection and debrief. Drawing on postdigital perspectives, the design positions GenAI as neither threat nor solution but as a provocation for identity work. Both critical evaluation of technology and self-knowledge matter more when AI can convincingly represent a person. Preliminary findings from this first iteration, drawn from facilitator reflections and de-identified conversation logs, suggest that the pedagogical value of self-representing avatars lies in the critical questioning they provoke, rather than in their technical sophistication. The workshop offers a practical, adaptable model for critical and creative engagement with GenAI and professional identity.

Organizations must combine clear downward direction with upward employee voice, and the age diversity of contemporary workforces is often presented as making this balance harder to achieve. This article examines that claim through an integrative review of research on organizational communication, employee voice and silence, psychological safety, organizational justice, and generational diversity. The review covers the four cohorts that dominate today's workforce (Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z), considers Generation Alpha prospectively, and sets boundaries for its central constructs: multigenerational workplace, downward and upward communication, communication balance, and communication equilibrium. Searches combined communication-direction, voice, and generation terms, supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of African journal platforms; sources were screened against explicit inclusion criteria, synthesized through data reduction, display, comparison, and verification, and each claim was graded as established, supported, or conjectural. Meta-analytic and consensus evidence shows that differences between generational cohorts in work attitudes are small and confounded with age and period effects. The article therefore proposes a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model (CEM), which starts from age diversity but locates its communicative effects in five proximal sources of variation: career stage, hierarchical role, digital access, work arrangement, and cultural orientation. The model specifies one downward condition (directive clarity), two upward conditions (psychological safety and leadership responsiveness), and one bidirectional condition (channel diversity), which together sustain directional balance, a state in which decision-makers act on clear direction and accurate upward information. Five assumptions underpin the model, and equilibrium is maintained by a balancing responsiveness loop that counters a reinforcing spiral of silence. Eight propositions, with indicators, levels of analysis, and evidential status, set out a research agenda that prioritizes designs separating age, period, and cohort effects and theory built from sub-Saharan African organizations, treating their employees as agents of voice rather than deviations from Northern norms.

BETTER 2040 is an immersive, interactive symposium that invites participants to explore the technological, epistemic, and ethical disruptions reshaping higher education in the age of generative AI. Set within the fictional University of Banford, participants engage with realistic leadership scenarios, collaborative decision-making, and strategic design challenges to examine trust, pedagogical innovation, and institutional transformation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

The rapid expansion of shared e-scooter services has introduced a novel public health challenge, with rising injury rates reported globally. Existing epidemiological studies rely largely on retrospective hospital or police records, which lack data on pre-crash mechanisms. While naturalistic studies have begun to fill this gap, they have thus far relied on associational measures that may be biased by confounding. This study aims to quantify the causal effects of rider behavior and environmental factors on e-scooter safety–critical events (SCEs) using a formal causal inference framework. We conducted a case-control analysis within a naturalistic riding study of a public e-scooter service in Gothenburg, Sweden (2022–2023), drawing from 6868 trips. Our analysis included 61 SCEs (cases) and 183 randomly selected control events. We used directed acyclic graphs to identify confounders and applied the parametric g-formula weighted for exposure duration to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences. After adjustment, the risk of an SCE increased substantially for single-handed riding (RR = 5.5), riding through an intersection (RR = 3.8), and inexperience (RR = 2.8). Phone use was associated with an approximately threefold increase in risk (RR = 3.1), though this estimate was not statistically significant. Both rider behavior (e.g., inexperience, single-handed riding) and the built environment (e.g., intersections) are significant causal contributors to e-scooter crash risk. These findings provide evidence for a multi-level public health strategy that focuses on novice rider education, infrastructure modifications at intersections, and technological interventions to support riders during their trips.

Although Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is grounded in principles of inclusion, flexibility, and learner variability, its implementation in higher education can become reduced to procedural or checklist-driven approaches, creating a tension between its human-centred philosophy and institutional practice. This paper adopts a reflective approach to examine the implementation of UDL across selected courses at an Australian university, exploring how shared understandings of inclusive teaching were co-constructed through dialogue between academics and an educational developer. The reflective inquiry suggests that meaningful UDL implementation is less dependent on frameworks than on relational, dialogic engagement through which pedagogical meaning is negotiated in context. At a time when higher education is increasingly shaped by digital technologies and artificial intelligence, the paper argues for re-centring relationships, collaboration, and human judgement as the foundation of meaningful curriculum transformation. In doing so, it positions educational developers as knowledge architects who facilitate the co-construction of inclusive pedagogical practice and offers a relational perspective on UDL implementation that may inform educational developers and academics seeking to implement inclusive curriculum renewal within their own institutional contexts.

Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Graduate employability has become a strategic priority across higher education, yet development of employability capabilities often remains fragmented, positioned outside the curriculum through co-curricular activities or graduate attribute frameworks that lack developmental coherence (Jackson & Bridgstock, 2021). This poster asks: how can employability capabilities be scaffolded longitudinally through reflective practice and Work-Integrated Learning to develop professional identity and career resilience in AI-enabled professional contexts? It presents the curriculum design rationale for the Bachelor of Applied Business at UNSW College, commencing October 2026, demonstrating how digital infrastructure, systematic reflection, and authentic workplace learning build career-ready graduates who work critically with emerging technologies. The design positions reflection not as an isolated assessment task but as career development pedagogy, building metacognitive capability, professional identity, and adaptive resilience across three years. This draws on foundational theories of reflective practice (Schön, 1992) and transformative learning (Mezirow, 1991), integrated with contemporary scholarship on professional identity formation (Jackson, 2016, 2017) and career adaptability (Savickas & Porfeli, 2012). The scaffolded architecture moves from foundational self-awareness tasks in Year 1, through applied workplace reflection during industry placements in Year 2, to integrative professional identity synthesis in the Year 3 capstone—providing authentic contexts for capability development throughout the degree. This progression is enabled through Canvas LMS integrated with the Stackle reflective learning platform. Stackle creates a longitudinal ePortfolio where students document reflective entries across all courses, receive structured prompts aligned to developmental focus, and build a cumulative narrative of professional growth. The curriculum embeds industry engagement through industry-informed assessment tasks across 100% of courses, formal placements, and a capstone industry project. Reflective practice is explicitly connected to each WIL experience through Stackle, requiring students to analyse workplace challenges and articulate capability development—an approach shown to strengthen pre-professional identity formation (Jackson, 2017; Trede et al., 2012). The platform enables integrated feedback from academic supervisors and industry mentors, making capability development visible to students, educators, and potential employers. Embedding AI fluency as a professional capability is central to this design. Rather than treating generative AI as peripheral or threatening to assessment integrity, the curriculum positions AI literacy as essential to contemporary professional practice. Students engage with transparent AI disclosure practices in reflection, use AI tools critically to analyse workplace data, and develop ethical reasoning frameworks for AI use. Assessment structures centre human judgment and applied problem-solving—reflective analysis, workplace challenge responses, and professional presentations—requiring critical thinking about AI outputs rather than uncritical acceptance. This responds to contemporary debates about authentic assessment in AI-mediated learning environments (Bearman et al., 2023), positioning graduates as professionals who work with AI critically and ethically. This poster presents: (1) the theoretical framework; (2) the three-year reflective practice progression model; (3) the WIL integration strategy with 100% industry-informed assessment; and (4) design principles for embedding AI fluency. The contribution is a replicable framework for embedding employability longitudinally while leveraging digital infrastructure to support human agency in AI-augmented professional contexts.

documents.abstract: Australian universities are revising generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) guidance under strong pressure to assure learning, academic integrity and assessment quality. This concise paper reports a public-source mapping of GenAI policy, assessment guidance and student AI-literacy preparation across the 38 Universities Australia member universities. Using six TEQSA sources as contextual material, 100 university sources were coded by authority level, dominant public guidance approach, assessment model and student-facing literacy support. The public evidence shows diverse policy configurations: 18 universities used a structured framework, scale, tier or lane model, while eight relied mainly on assessment-specific rules. Student preparation was also prominent: 19 universities provided formal AI-specific learning opportunities, and 12 provided structured student hubs or toolkits. The findings suggest that GenAI policy can function as curriculum infrastructure rather than only academic-integrity compliance. The paper contributes to Human-Centred Learning Design by treating GenAI policy as learning design infrastructure that connects assessment authority, student trust, feedback expectations and AI literacy.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally altered how learners access, construct, and engage with knowledge. Existing discussions of GenAI literacy have largely emphasised operational competencies, such as prompt engineering, understanding AI capabilities, and ethical use. While these competencies remain important, they do not fully address the epistemic challenges arising from AI-mediated knowledge production. This paper proposes reframing GenAI literacy through the lens of epistemic agency; that is, learners’ capacity to critically evaluate, regulate, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge generated in collaboration with intelligent systems. Rather than viewing GenAI literacy as a collection of technical skills, this conceptual paper argues that its primary educational purpose is to cultivate learners who can exercise informed judgement in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments. Building on existing AI literacy scholarship and theories of epistemic agency, the paper introduces a conceptual framework comprising four interrelated dimensions: epistemic evaluation, epistemic regulation, epistemic responsibility, and epistemic autonomy. The framework provides a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding how GenAI literacy can move beyond operational competence towards fostering independent, reflective, and responsible knowledge construction.

Embodied foundation models produce impressive demonstrations, but executing long, complex tasks depends on software outside the model, just as in the ransition from ChatGPT to Codex. We call that software the embodied agent harness and divide it into planning, skill acquisition, memory, monitoring, and self-evolution. The papers come from robotics, machine learning, and embodied-AI venues, 2022--2026. About a fifth of the citations are preprints or non-archival manuscripts, mostly for new directions. Open problems remain in efficiency, robustness, generalizability, model availability, multi-robot orchestration, and evaluation.

Assessment in data visualisation courses too often rewards technical output over communicating substance. When visualisation is taught as a tool rather than a discipline, students learn to produce work that meets the brief but has little to say. This paper reports on a course redesign that addresses this gap through a human-centred assessment design grounded in evaluative judgement theory, treating evaluative judgement as a capability exercised by both students and markers. The redesign is structured around five elements addressing student ownership of project topics, portfolio assessment, descriptive capability levels, practitioner modelling, and creative freedom within a structured framework, implemented in a required course within a Master of Data Science program. Practitioner inquiry into the operation of this design in the presence of generative AI revealed that AI functioned not as a threat to academic integrity but as a mechanism that raised creative ambition, shifting the limiting factor from technical skill to evaluative judgement. Although situated in a data visualisation course, the contribution is broader. As generative AI makes technical production easier, helping students develop the capacity to recognise, justify, and communicate insight becomes the central challenge across higher education, and this paper suggests one way to address it.

The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has accelerated institutional investment in AI infrastructure, yet many universities continue to face difficulties translating institutional strategy into consistent subject-level teaching practice. This paper presents a School-level framework developed at an Australian university. The paper reports the design rationale, outputs and approved deployment model of the framework, including staff capability resources, configurable AI templates, disclosure mechanisms and governance processes. Informed by Educational Design Research and scholarship on organisational change in education, the paper argues that Schools can serve as meso-level environments that enact institutional AI strategy through resources and structures designed to support subject-level teaching practice. It contributes a meso-level governance model, six transferable design principles, and an operational framework intended to support responsible and human-centred AI-supported learning. Formal evaluation is planned following the pilot phase.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Technical job interviews place computing students under pressure to demonstrate algorithmic and communication skills simultaneously under live observation, producing what we term the articulation gap. Existing preparation pathways provide only partial support: coding platforms ignore communication, coaching is economically inaccessible, and current AI simulators remain reactive. We present AIView, a multi-agent conversational platform that scaffolds integrated interview competencies. A LangGraph orchestrator coordinates specialised agents for question delivery and adaptive guidance alongside verbalisation monitors and an affect-aware tone layer, with assessments anchored in the SOLO taxonomy. An evaluation with 31 students showed high usability (SUS = 73.8), strong trust in AI feedback (M = 3.94), and high recommendation intent (M = 4.29). Participants valued personalised, code-aware feedback and a low-pressure learning environment. By fostering compassionate human-AI collaboration that supports creative problem solving and connection in a digital learning environment, AIView represents a step towards democratising access to career preparation through adaptive scaffolding.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Esta pesquisa analisou a incorporação de um módulo multimodal de inteligência artificial (IA), o Acelerador de Catalogação, a um sistema de gestão de bibliotecas, com objetivo central de considerar o impacto dessa ferramenta na rotina de processamento técnico, avaliando a eficiência operacional, a precisão da extração de dados e a facilidade de uso, com especial atenção à preservação da soberania técnica do bibliotecário. Realizou-se um estudo de caso quali-quantitativo em ambiente real de trabalho, com 12 bibliotecários voluntários experientes em catalogação tradicional. Os dados quantitativos, extraídos automaticamente pelo sistema, compararam 52 registros do regime tradicional e 64 do regime assistido por IA; os dados qualitativos vieram de um fórum de diálogo colaborativo, contido como ferramenta do próprio software com recursos de interação e engajamento, este fórum foi subdividido em cinco eixos temáticos, tratado por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados evidenciaram uma redução média por título que caiu 32,5% (de 10 min 13 s para 6 min 54 s) e a completude aumentou 24,5% (de 23,6 para 29,4 campos preenchidos). A IA foi eficaz em tarefas mimeomórficas (ações mecânicas, repetitivas e estruturadas), enquanto as tarefas polimórficas, que exigem julgamento contextual, tratamento de exceções e adequação a políticas locais, permaneceram com o profissional, porém com sugestões do agente de IA. Observou-se maior incidência de edições posteriores ao cadastro no regime assistido (11 em 64 processos, contra 2 em 52), concentrada em um catalogador e em obras jurídicas. Os participantes descreveram a tecnologia como “assistente sob comando”, o que sustenta a curadoria humana como componente estrutural do fluxo. Concluiu-se que o ganho de eficiência convive com a preservação da autoridade técnica e do protagonismo do bibliotecário.

This study examines how awareness of generative AI academic integrity policies shapes student anxiety, ethical reasoning, and writing practices in higher education. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of student discourse from YouTube and Reddit, the study explores how detection-oriented governance frameworks are experienced and negotiated outside formal institutional contexts. Findings indicate that students do not primarily describe intentional rule-breaking; instead, they articulate experiences of surveillance, uncertainty, and adaptation within assessment systems perceived as inconsistent and adversarial. Three interrelated themes are identified: surveillance anxiety and defensive authorship; normative dissonance and moral negotiation of AI use; and cognitive offloading, systemic strain, and declining trust in assessment integrity. Across these themes, AI policy awareness is shown to shape not only behavioural responses but also students’ affective and epistemic relationships with writing, authorship, and institutional authority. The study argues that detection-first approaches risk intensifying anxiety and undermining trust without resolving underlying tensions in assessment design. It concludes that generative AI exposes structural fragilities in higher education, suggesting the need to reorient academic integrity governance toward design-led, transparent, and equity-sensitive approaches that prioritise learning, trust, and student experience.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human decision-making under uncertainty faces growing challenges from information-based threats that pose risks to human cognitive processes and behaviour. Although their potential harm is widely acknowledged, there remains no well-defined construct for characterising the degree to which information-based threats influence changes in human judgments and decision-making, impeding theoretical advancement, measurement, and effective countermeasure development. Here, we introduce a human cognitive security construct focused on linking information-based threats to observable outcomes to bridge field-level definitions with operational measures by drawing from core mechanisms related to information processing and decision-making. To connect the information environment to behaviour, we develop an integrative modelling framework that unifies Bayesian inference with affect-modulated decision valuation, capturing how cognitive resource allocation and affective valuation shape three core behavioural outcomes: veracity discernment, task-oriented actions, and information sharing. Through computational simulations, we demonstrate that this framework can explain canonical phenomena, including cognitive heuristics and incongruent veracity discernment and sharing behaviour, and we test model predictions against empirical data of the illusory truth effect (R² = 0.86). To guide future empirical examinations, we propose empirically grounded behavioural outcome measures of cognitive security and outline how environment-specific elements, characterised by data availability and ecological constraints, affect individuals’ cognitive security.

documents.abstract: Marking is among the most time-consuming activities in education, and artificial intelligence (AI) is widely proposed as a remedy. Attention has centred on generative large language models, yet regulators raise concerns about their bias, consistency, and explainability. This paper contrasts generative grading with per-question classification models trained only on an educator’s own marking and deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow. The architectures are compared against criteria drawn from regulatory guidance: transparency, construct-relevant features, determinism, and specifiable training data. A narrower role for generative models is also identified, in composing and restructuring marker-approved feedback rather than in marking. Deployment analytics from one platform are then reported, covering approximately 166,000 marked questions, 39,500 essays, and six institutions: 66.2% of questions were marked in under one minute, 77.6% to 89.5% of AI suggestions were accepted, and essay models reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.93 for high-confidence predictions. Questionnaire responses from earlier pilots (33 markers, 30 students) are also reported: markers described marking as faster and consistent feedback as easier to provide; most students rated feedback more consistent and higher in quality. Implications for institutions selecting or building such tools are discussed, alongside the limitations of vendor-collected data.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering universities not only as a student-owned productivity tool but as part of the digital infrastructure through which learning support, feedback and assessment guidance are mediated. This concise paper reports on an exploratory pilot of Cogniti AI agents in an Aotearoa New Zealand foundation business course, with a focus on human-centred learning design. The pilot involved five role-specialised agents: a course buddy for administration support, a case-discussion agent for Maori entrepreneurship learning, and three virtual team members focused on task coordination, relationship management and value-adding contribution. Rather than positioning AI as a generic chatbot, the paper presents a design model for embedding AI agents within the course ecosystem. Drawing on design records, early usage patterns and practice reflections, the paper argues that AI agents can extend human-centred pedagogy when they are co-created with students, shaped by student input, assessment-aligned, and circumscribed by teacher oversight. The contribution is a practical model for integrating AI agents into learning management systems in ways that prioritise connection, mentorship, evaluative judgement, feedback literacy and collaborative learning.

Higher education students are incorporating generative artificial intelligence into many aspects of their studies, yet the ways they judge its positive and negative impacts remain poorly understood. Using qualitative content analysis supported by code-frequency analysis, this paper examines open-ended comments from 2,802 participants drawn from a survey of 8,021 students across four Australian universities. Reported impacts clustered around four themes: study practices, quality, efficiency, and institutional practices. Positive impacts were more frequently coded overall, particularly when students described using AI to support their own study practices and efficiency. Negative responses centred on the inaccuracy of AI outputs. Although relatively few participants commented on institutional teaching and assessment practices, these responses were predominantly negative. The findings suggest that students value AI not only for the quality of its outputs, but also for its role in helping them begin, continue, refine, and complete academic work. Rather than uncritically accepting or categorically rejecting AI, students appeared to make situated judgements about its usefulness and limitations, shaped by concerns about accuracy and trust, as well as by the agency and control they retained over its use. Institutional responses should therefore engage with the complexity of students’ practices and the conditions under which they perceive AI to be useful or problematic.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of students’ everyday study practices, yet institutional debate still tends to position it as either an efficiency tool or an academic-integrity threat. This binary framing obscures a more educationally useful question: can AI be designed to help students engage meaningfully with difficult concepts while helping educators see where understanding breaks down? This project evaluates a course-tailored AI learning assistant embedded in a large undergraduate course at an Australian public university. The tool was bounded to authoritative course materials and instructor-provided resources. Students could ask questions, receive course-grounded answers and explanations, and clarify or organise their understanding without having assessed tasks completed for them. Informed by self-determination theory and cognitive load theory, the design sought to support competence and autonomy, reduce unnecessary cognitive burden, and provide low-stakes help at the moment of uncertainty (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Sweller, 1988). Students were randomly assigned either access to the tool or standard course resources. Evaluation drew on complementary sources of evidence gathered across the teaching period, combining students’ own accounts of their experience with routinely captured indicators of engagement and achievement. The evidence points in a consistent direction. Students with access reported a more positive orientation towards their study and towards the responsible institutional use of AI. Their engagement shifted in character rather than in volume, suggesting sustained attention to core course materials rather than a general increase in undifferentiated digital activity. Indications for achievement were encouraging, particularly for students at greater risk of not succeeding, although the strength of these signals varied. An equally important feature lay in the questions themselves. Patterns in students’ questions made recurring misconceptions and points of uncertainty more visible to the educator. This supported more responsive teaching: explanations, examples, and follow-up support could be focused on what students were actually struggling to understand. The initiative therefore created a two-way pedagogical feedback loop. Students received immediate, course-aligned support for working through concepts, while the educator gained diagnostic insight into learning needs not always visible in conventional analytics or classroom participation. The project locates compassion in the design choices, not in the technology itself. Course alignment, bounded assistance, student choice, and attention to digital burden offer a way for AI to support conceptual engagement without displacing core resources or student agency (Burr et al., 2020; Holmes et al., 2022). The resulting principles are to ground AI in authoritative course materials, preserve the integrity of assessed work, enable low-stakes questioning, use question patterns to inform teaching, and evaluate wellbeing alongside engagement and achievement. These principles are applicable across disciplines and tertiary contexts.

documents.abstract: To address the problems of decontextualized vocabulary drills and the lack of adaptive, data-informed instruction, this study designs and evaluates a web-based gamified vocabulary system integrating an adaptive task sequencing algorithm, real-time learning analytics, and multimodal scenarios within a constructivist framework. In a 16-week quasi-experiment with 200 non-English-major undergraduates, the experimental group (n = 100) improved by 22.5 points in total vocabulary score, in comparison with an improvement of 11.3 points in the control group (n = 100), with the largest gains made in low-frequency word mastery (+41.5%) and vocabulary application (+39.6%). The experimental group also reported higher intrinsic motivation (4.32 vs. 3.56, p < .001), and platform logs showed task completion rising from 78.6% to 93.8% and error rate falling from 28.4% to 10.1%. Two teachers used the dashboard for data-informed instructional adjustments. These findings illustrate how web-based learning technologies can support learner autonomy and instructional decision-making in higher education.

Trustworthiness in artificial intelligence depends not only on what a model decides, but also on how it handles and explains cases in which a reliable decision cannot be made. In critical domains such as healthcare and finance, a reject option allows the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient, making it essential to explain why an instance is rejected in order to support informed human intervention. In these settings, explanations must not only be interpretable, but also faithful to the underlying model and computationally efficient enough to support real-time decision making. Abductive explanations guarantee fidelity, but their exact computation is known to be NP-hard for many classes of models, limiting their practical applicability. Computing minimum-size abductive explanations is an even more challenging problem, as it requires reasoning not only about fidelity but also about optimality. Prior work has addressed this challenge in restricted settings, including log-linear-time algorithms for computing minimum-size abductive explanations in linear models without rejection, as well as a polynomial-time method based on linear programming for computing abductive explanations, without guarantees of minimum size, for linear models with a reject option. In this work, we bridge these lines of research by computing minimum-size abductive explanations for linear models with a reject option. For accepted instances, we adapt the log-linear algorithm to efficiently compute optimal explanations. For rejected instances, we formulate a 0–1 integer linear programming problem that characterizes minimum-size abductive explanations of rejection. Although this formulation is NP-hard in theory, our experimental results show that it is consistently more efficient in practice than the linear-programming-based approach that does not guarantee minimum-size explanations.

Proactive multimodal AI can watch a user's screen, listen to speech, track interaction, and decide whether to enter unfolding work. Little is known about how people want to control what such AI may perceive and how far it may participate. Informed by a 14-person Wizard-of-Oz study, we built SpotMe, a design probe that senses screen, speech, and interaction; chooses Silence, Ask, or Assist; and lets users separately configure what it may perceive, how far it may participate, and what types of support it may provide. In a 16-person study on a civic dashboard, participants first experienced proactive help, then inspected decisions to act or remain silent, and then configured SpotMe's perception and participation. We found that participants could keep all perception channels available while lowering participation to Ask or Silence; that exposing suppressed decisions made silence interpretable and contestable; and that seeing what SpotMe used led some to change how they clicked, highlighted, and spoke. We contribute an empirical account of inspecting and controlling proactive multimodal AI by decoupling perception from participation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are increasingly being adopted in higher education; however, limited research has examined their pedagogical integration within learning environments. This paper reports findings from an exploratory mixed-methods case study of a GenAI chatbot embedded in a postgraduate unit at an Australian university. Designed as a pedagogically embedded learning companion, the chatbot provided contextualised guidance and functioned as a first point of contact for students seeking clarification and support. Findings indicate that students perceived the chatbot as a useful and accessible learning resource that supported engagement, reflection, and self-directed learning. Three themes emerged: first-contact pedagogical support, AI-mediated scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. Students valued the immediacy and contextual relevance of responses while recognising the continuing importance of educator guidance. These initial findings provide insights into the design of pedagogically embedded GenAI learning companions and their potential role in supporting learning within higher education.

documents.abstract: Developing communication skills remains a core challenge in higher education, particularly in providing scalable opportunities for practice and feedback. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated systems function as interactive learning environments for communication skills development. Two implementations are examined: a voice-only conversational AI-mediated system used across health disciplines and a digital human avatar used in a business unit. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative survey data and qualitative content. Findings highlighted three key affordances: repeated low-stakes practice, immediate feedback, and flexible engagement. Students reported increased confidence and perceived skill development. Limitations included conversational inaccuracies, realism, technical reliability, and feedback consistency. Importantly, findings indicate that the effectiveness of AI systems is strongly influenced by prompt design, scenario construction, and alignment with learner level. This paper reframes AI tools not as autonomous technologies, but as designed interactive learning environments requiring careful pedagogical integration. Implications are discussed for the design of AI-supported learning activities, particularly in contexts involving oral communication and authentic assessment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Where does meaningful learning begin in an era of generative artificial intelligence (AI)? Current responses to AI in higher education have largely focused on assessment redesign, academic integrity and AI literacy. While these developments have strengthened assessment practice, they often assume that meaningful learning begins when students enter university. This paper argues that responding effectively to AI requires reconsidering this assumption. Drawing upon the learning beyond the classroom framework, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy for assessment design that recognises learners’ existing educational resources and supports their development into disciplinary judgement. This paper contributes in three ways. First, it introduces the learning beyond the classroom framework as a conceptual foundation for understanding learning in AI-mediated higher education. Second, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy that connects recognition, translation, transformation and disciplinary judgement within a developmental approach to assessment design. Third, it translates this philosophy into five practical principles that provide educators with a flexible lens for redesigning assessment across diverse disciplinary contexts. Rather than treating AI as the central educational challenge, the paper positions it as a catalyst for reconsidering the purposes of assessment, arguing that higher education’s enduring contribution lies in cultivating critical judgement, ethical reasoning and meaningful contribution.

In technology disciplines, students are more engaged and better prepared for employment when they experience technical work as purposeful professional practice rather than as isolated exercises (Kerven et al., 2017). Generative AI can now produce working code, configured systems and polished documentation, so students can complete tasks that mainly ask for these outputs without doing much of the work themselves. Such tasks are unlikely to hold students’ interest, and the work submitted can be weak evidence of capability. The professional judgement remains theirs: deciding what should be built, for whom, within which constraints, and with what consequences. The challenge for curriculum design is to integrate, teach and assess that judgement. This presentation describes a curriculum design we developed in response. Each unit is set in one authentic workplace context, the anchor scenario, which defines the stakeholders, constraints and outcome for the whole unit. Every session then presents a session scenario: a professional decision in that context, building on the one before. In the final assessment, students deliver the outcome the anchor scenario set. Content is taught when students need it for a decision, and assessment is set in the same context. The approach draws on situated learning, in which judgement develops through authentic activity in realistic contexts (Brown et al., 1989; Lave & Wenger, 1991), and on Action Mapping, which begins from a real workplace outcome and derives the decisions learners must make before selecting content (Moore, 2017). Narrative carries more force when scenarios accumulate rather than stand alone (Bruner, 1991). Sustained scenario structures have precedents: anchored instruction centres on one extended problem (Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt, 1990), media computation organises content coverage (Guzdial, 2003), and task-driven case studies guide practice rather than judgement (Porubän et al., 2024). None spans an entire unit while structuring cumulative professional decisions, producing employer-facing artefacts, and giving AI a purposeful role. Each unit is built in three phases. The Anchor phase derives the scenario from a workplace outcome and produces a unit design plan mapping outcomes to assessments and giving every session its own scenario. The Embed phase scripts each session in full, writing assessments at the same time and checking alignment in both directions (Biggs, 1996), with every activity carrying a short connection back to the scenario. The Shift phase builds the design as web-based learning paths for delivery on campus, online or in hybrid mode. This approach now runs in more than 30 units across five discipline areas. They include a café point-of-sale system built over 11 programming sessions, a hospital network designed for a computer networking unit, and a robotic warehouse floor for an electrical engineering unit. The presentation walks through the designs themselves, alongside feedback from the teaching staff who delivered them. While the scenarios are varied, each design begins with the professional world and its people, derives the decisions from them, and lets the technology find its place inside that world.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education by reshaping how learners generate ideas, solve problems, and engage in creative knowledge construction. While existing research has primarily examined the effectiveness of AI tools on learning outcomes, writing performance, and student engagement, comparatively little attention has been paid to understanding how educators intentionally design AI-assisted creative learning experiences. This paper presents a scoping review of 49 empirical and conceptual sources on AI-assisted creativity in higher education to identify recurring instructional design practices, human–AI interaction patterns, and pedagogical strategies. Rather than focusing on technological capabilities alone, the review synthesizes how creative learning activities are structured around collaboration between learners, educators, and AI systems, while also engaging directly with mixed evidence on AI’s creative value, including findings that AI-assisted ideation can expand idea novelty under some conditions, yet produce design fixation and narrowed divergent thinking under others. Building upon this synthesis, the paper proposes a preliminary Human-Centered AI Creativity Design (HACD) framework that positions AI as a collaborative creative partner while preserving learner agency, critical reflection, and ethical decision-making. The framework offers an initial conceptual model to guide educators in designing meaningful AI-supported creative learning experiences and provides a foundation for empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support technical program managers in identifying delivery risks, but improved productivity does not necessarily imply more complete risk recognition. A critical failure mode arises when a manager initially identifies a material risk and later removes it after encountering an AI-generated assessment. This paper develops a human–AI decision-comparison method for detecting such omissions without equating disagreement with error. The framework records an unaided initial risk register, randomly assigns decision makers to a human-only second pass, ordinary AI assistance, or AI assistance with a structured challenge step, and assesses final decisions against independently adjudicated scenario risks. It distinguishes risk discovery, risk retention, and severity-weighted coverage using explicit transition measures and a multilevel comparison strategy. Domain-specific scenarios span cloud migration, data platforms, regulated delivery, and automotive system validation. The contribution is a reproducible measurement architecture for identifying whether AI assistance is associated with excess removal of risks that were previously recognized. The paper specifies testable causal contrasts and validity controls; it does not claim that an experiment has already been conducted.

This poster positions digital media (DM) assets as pedagogical decisions, arguing that their value lies not in technical sophistication, but in how effectively a medium supports learning within a given educational context (Mayer, 2020). Aligned with the ASCILITE 2026 subtheme of Human Centred Learning Design, this work introduces Digital Media as Pedagogy (DMaP), a decision-making approach that supports intentional DM selection in higher education. DMaP foregrounds pedagogical relationships and learner needs over technology guided choice, demonstrating that the suitability of different media forms varies depending on learning outcomes and the specific educational context. Meaningful media decision making requires strong collaboration between Learning Experience Designers (LEDs) and DM teams. Media design is frequently treated as a production task, downstream of the core learning content design (Thompson & Harris, 2025). This limits pedagogically aligned innovation positioning media specialists as technical implementers rather than pedagogical collaborators. Research on educational video and DM highlights that design decisions such as pacing, length, and interactivity, have a greater impact on engagement and learning than technical, even aesthetic, sophistication (Guo et al., 2014). This poster reframes the LED/DM relationship as a critical collaborative practice where expertise in pedagogy, accessibility, analytics and media production intersect. Early and ongoing collaboration supports more intentional and sustainable media design. This approach has informed changes to practice, including earlier involvement of DM specialists in subject development meetings. Positioning DM teams within early pedagogical discussions enables more cohesive alignment between learning intent and media, moving away from a more transactional style of interaction between LEDs and DM team members. The DMaP approach integrates five interconnected design lenses. The lens of pedagogical intent draws on Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) to examine whether a medium is pedagogically appropriate for specific content and learner contexts, while also legitimising collaboration across pedagogical, technological, and content expertise (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The Cognitive Engagement lens applies the ICAP framework to examine observable learner activity, recognising that passive, active, constructive, and interactive modes each have contextual pedagogical value rather than forming a simple hierarchy (Chi & Wylie, 2014). Accessibility and Inclusion are foregrounded through Universal Design for Learning (UDL), positioning flexibility and learner choice as pedagogical strengths. This is realised through multiple means of engagement, representation and action and expressions (CAST 2024). Evidence-based Tool Selection draws on research demonstrating that digital media effectiveness varies significantly by context and design rather than novelty and considers pedagogical soundness and institutional viability (Kirkwood & Price, 2014). The final lens examines Integration and Learning Systems, recognising that, from our experience, media effectiveness appears to be influenced by LMS integration and breaks from cognitive load. DMaP questions the conventional matching of digital tool to task which tends to favour novelty over pedagogical fit. Instead, it proposes a human centred decision logic where media is selected because it aligns with intended cognitive engagement. A pedagogical approach to digital media enables accessible participation and remains feasible within institutional constraints. DMaP offers an appliable, theoretically informed approach for learning designers and DM teams.

La irrupción de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la escuela suele leerse desde dos posiciones simétricas: la adopción instrumental y la prohibición defensiva. El objetivo de este artículo es proponer un marco teórico-metodológico que supere ese dilema desde una institución educativa rural de baja conectividad en Cajibío, Cauca (Colombia). Se trata de un artículo de reflexión derivado de una tesis doctoral en curso, elaborado mediante análisis hermenéutico-conceptual de fuentes de la deconstrucción, la teoría de sistemas sociales, la crítica de la digitalidad y las epistemologías del Sur, contrastadas con antecedentes empíricos recientes sobre inteligencia artificial generativa, educación y ruralidad y traducidas en un diseño de investigación basada en diseño. Como resultado se construyen tres conceptos articulados: la superficialidad cognitiva, entendida como procesamiento del saber sin reingreso; la deconstrucción digital, operación breve y situada que irrita esa superficialidad a través de la interfaz algorítmica; y las digitalidades deconstructivas, estado plural en el que la reducción de la superficialidad se vuelve expectativa del sistema escolar. Se propone, además, la noción de acoplamiento pharmaco-deconstructivo, según la cual la decisión pedagógica no versa sobre adoptar o prohibir, sino sobre regular la dosis de irritación, y un diseño de contraste con tres condiciones, reporte estratificado y criterios de refutación declarados de antemano. Se concluye que la escasez de conectividad, leída como lugar de enunciación y no como déficit, exige pensar la mediación docente asincrónica como condición de una justicia cognitiva situada.

LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

Explainable AI (XAI) methods are commonly evaluated using functional correctness metrics, also called faithfulness or fidelity, which estimate how closely an explanation reflects the model’s reasoning. Higher correctness is assumed to produce better human understanding, but this link has not been tested with controlled levels. We conducted a user study ( N = 200 ) that manipulated explanation correctness at four levels (100%, 85%, 70%, 55%) in a synthetic time series classification task where participants could not rely on domain knowledge or visual intuition. Explanations were constructed to resemble feature attributions, with correctness defined against a known ground truth rather than estimated from a trained model. Participants predicted a simulated AI’s decisions from these explanations (forward simulation), and we used their forward simulation accuracy as a proxy for understanding. Correctness affected forward simulation accuracy, but not at every level: accuracy dropped at 70% and 55% relative to 100%, with no further reduction below 70% and no conclusive difference between 85% and 100%. Lower correctness reduced how many participants predicted accurately rather than lowering accuracy uniformly, and even with fully correct explanations, only a subset of participants predicted well above chance. In exploratory analyses, some participants predicted decisions accurately but described the wrong pattern when asked what the AI used, and self-reported ratings correlated with forward simulation accuracy only when explanations were fully correct. These findings suggest that, for feature-attribution-style explanations, not all differences in functional correctness translate to differences in human understanding, highlighting the need to validate functional metrics against human outcomes.

The use of generative AI (GenAI) technologies has become increasingly prevalent across Australian higher education. As these tools become an integral part of learning, they also raise concerns about over-reliance and learner agency (Resnick, 2024), authorship, ownership, and problematic forms of co-creation (Bozkurt, 2024). In Australia, 31% of the student population identify as having English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) (Australian Government Department of Education, 2024). Apart from cultural and linguistic challenges, EAL/D students also need to adapt to new academic expectations and practices that account for the impacts of GenAI technologies (Kebble, 2023). Given the unique challenges facing EAL/D student cohorts with their diverse pre-existing technological backgrounds, a gap exists in understanding how EAL/D students perceive their own work and academic contributions in relation to their use of GenAI tools. This study explores EAL/D students’ AI-assisted learning experiences and perspectives on agency through qualitative interviews conducted with 34 Master of Digital Communication students over 18 months. Findings suggest that EAL/D students are instinctively adjusting and adapting their learning practices as they engage with these technologies and making agentic decisions that support their learning. To maintain what they considered to be original and creative in their work, students developed several strategies to distinguish their own work from AI-generated output. We also found that as EAL/D students’ engagement with AI increases, they develop critical self-scrutiny. They maintain agency and ownership over their assessed work by ensuring that their (human) creativity remains central throughout the learning process. While there are some commonalities, the students in our study took diverse paths, with some students developing more nuanced and balanced approaches to using AI than others. For these students, the shift enabled them to integrate GenAI strategically while maintaining their own voice and sense of agency.

Stress management in higher education often emphasizes individual self-regulation. Less is known about how spatial configuration and ambient feedback shape mutual awareness and psychological comfort during co-located relaxation. This paper presents EchoBreset, a shared dyadic biofeedback prototype that embeds respiration sensing and ambient lighting feedback into a campus-embedded relaxation booth. We report an exploratory mixed-methods study with 108 university participants in 54 dyads, each experiencing one of three seating configurations in a semi-controlled setting. The study examined perceived relaxation, respiratory-cycle duration similarity, completion of shared progress based on both partners’ cumulative breathing contributions, and reported social interaction. Across configurations, self-report measures showed significant pre-post reductions in state anxiety and increases in relaxation ratings, while between-configuration differences in change scores were not significant. Descriptively, side-by-side seating generally showed greater respiratory-cycle duration similarity and had the highest shared-progress completion rate. It was also the most frequently mentioned preference in post-session reflections. Face-to-face seating increased partner visibility but could introduce gaze-related discomfort, whereas back-to-back seating reduced social exposure but limited access to partner cues. Participants described using partner feedback to adjust breathing, although some reported performance pressure when attempting to match a partner or track shared progress. The findings yield four design considerations: providing partner cues without requiring sustained direct gaze, clarifying the distinct roles of immediate feedback and shared progress, balancing feedback salience to support selective attention, and encouraging joint participation without imposing performance requirements. This design case contributes empirically grounded design knowledge on spatial configuration, feedback interpretation, and flexibility in attention and participation for balancing mutual awareness and psychological comfort during collaborative breathing.

Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4–8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

Background: Clinical reasoning is a core competency in emergency medicine, and its structured teaching remains challenging. Generative artificial intelligence (ChatGPT) may represent a useful educational tool, but its impact on learning consolidation beyond immediate benefit remains uncertain. We assessed whether guided use of ChatGPT improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance without compromising its retention over time. Methods: A single-center, two-arm, parallel-group, exploratory randomized controlled trial was conducted in the emergency department of Mohammed VI University Hospital, Marrakech, Morocco. Sixty medical students (5th–6th year) were randomized 1:1, using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes generated by an independent investigator, to a ChatGPT group (simulated clinical cases with guided GPT-4o assistance) or a control group (no assistance); outcome assessors were blinded to group and time point, although participants could not be blinded to the intervention received. The primary outcome was the total Revised-IDEA (R-IDEA) score (/10), measured immediately after the intervention (T0) and again one month later under unassisted conditions (T1), analyzed by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusted for the T0 score. Results: All 60 participants were followed at T0 and T1, with no loss to follow-up. At T0, the R-IDEA score was significantly higher in the ChatGPT group (median 9.50 vs 8.50; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). At T1, the pattern reversed: the ChatGPT group showed a significant decline (median Δ = −0.75), whereas the control group improved (Δ = +1.00; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). ANCOVA confirmed a group effect at T1 favoring the control group (adjusted difference = 0.48 points, 95% CI 0.16–0.80; p = 0.004; partial η² = 0.136). Perceived confidence and benefit in the ChatGPT group were not correlated with actual performance change. Conclusions: Conclusions: Guided ChatGPT assistance improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance, but this benefit does not persist at one month and is accompanied by poorly calibrated learner confidence. These findings support structured pedagogical oversight of generative AI in medical education, combined with active learning-consolidation strategies to ensure durable skill acquisition.
